questions.question: What is fine-tuning generally most reliable for?
options: Teaching a model brand-new facts it can recall perfectly on demand
Adjusting a model's behavior, style, tone, or specializing it on a narrow task
Making a model faster to run at inference time
Increasing a model's context window size
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning is well-suited to shaping behavior, tone, format adherence, and task specialization, but is not a reliable way to teach a model to accurately recall specific new facts on demand.

questions.question: A team wants a model to accurately answer questions about pricing that changes weekly. Why is fine-tuning a poor fit here?
options: Fine-tuning is always more expensive than any other option in every situation
Fine-tuning bakes information into static weights, requiring expensive retraining every time the facts change, whereas retrieval (RAG) can serve fresh facts immediately
Fine-tuning cannot be used for any factual question
Weekly changes are too infrequent for any method to handle
questions.explanation: Frequently changing facts are better served by retrieving fresh information at request time (RAG) than by fine-tuning, which would require repeated, costly retraining to stay current.

questions.question: A team says 'the model doesn't know our internal terminology, let's fine-tune it.' Which question best diagnoses whether fine-tuning is the right fix?
options: Should we just start fine-tuning immediately without further discussion?
Is this actually a factual knowledge gap (better solved by RAG) or a behavior/style problem (better solved by fine-tuning)?
Why does the model need any specialized knowledge at all?
Can we avoid this decision by using a smaller model instead?
questions.explanation: Distinguishing between a knowledge gap (favoring retrieval/RAG) and a behavior gap (favoring fine-tuning) is the key diagnostic question, since fine-tuning is frequently misapplied to problems that are actually about missing or stale factual information.
